question: does allocating less during the load reduce what a serving process keeps resident
answer: no; it reduces time to first answer

environment.runtime: Docker Desktop 29.1.3, linux/arm64 VM, 10 CPU, 8.2 GB

dataset.note: one published generation, byte-identical across every arm: the snapshot format did not change between the two commits

go_accounting_over_the_same_range.note: measured on darwin by benchmarks/snapshot-heap, which is Go runtime accounting rather than resident pages

findings: The load allocates 60.5 MB less and the serving process keeps the same pages resident. 71.76 MB against 71.22 MB per server, 0.75 % apart over three pairs, where the arithmetic of the allocation removed would predict a drop of about thirty.

The reason is what transient means to an allocator: pages dirtied while decoding are handed back to the heap and reused by the work that follows, so they were never resident at steady state. Private_Dirty sampled after 4000 warmup calls and 2000 measured ones reports the settled serving heap, not the peak of the load.
What the work bought is the time to that first answer: 138-156 ms against 191-292 ms, three pairs of three, which matches the 123.6 ms against 134.5 ms the load benchmark measures directly on darwin.

Bytes per symbol did not move either: 647.348 before, 647.104 after, against the 800 B gate of LUQUE-2006. A corpus of 117,499 symbols sits at 72 MB per process, and the reason that is below the 100 MB reopen condition of LUQUE-2008 is the size of this corpus, not this work: the 94-98 MB previously recorded was over 161,819 symbols, which is 609 B per symbol against these 647.
limitations: This is not the reference host. The declared distribution target is linux/amd64 and this ran on a linux/arm64 VM under Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon; what makes the resident figures comparable in units is the 4096-byte page size, which matches, and what makes them comparable to each other is that both arms ran in the same VM against the same file.

Latency from a container is not comparable to the reference environment and no latency gate is claimed here. The first-answer figures are used only as a before/after ratio inside this VM. One p99 check of the harness failed at 4 clients in the full sweep (1.064 ms against a 1.000 ms allowance) and the harness did not emit its gate; a container with virtualised mounts is not where that limit is decided.

Peak resident during the load was not measured, only the settled value. A machine that starts several servers at once pays a peak this benchmark does not report, and that is the one place the removed allocation could still show.
Three pairs. Enough to say the resident difference is under one percent and that the first answer is consistently faster, not enough for a percentile.
